claims.source: We found, however, that the mean neural cancellation time for Movement cells was slightly earlier than that for Stop cells.
claims.evidence: This is a timing comparison between cell types.

claims.claim: Stop-related activity preceded the earliest stop-related truncation of EMG activity by a mere 10 ms.
claims.source: Moreover, Stop-related activity preceded the earliest stop-related truncation of EMG activity by a mere 10 ms.
claims.evidence: This is a timing comparison between neural and muscle activity.

claims.claim: The STN is part of the network in which visual attention and the salience of events are implemented.
claims.source: Indeed, the STN is part of the network in which visual attention and the salience of events are implemented (Baunez and Robbins, 1997; Baunez et al., 2007; Bočková et al., 2011; Schmalbach et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: 43% of cells with short-latency stop responses responded similarly or more strongly with sudden action initiation in switch-go trials.
claims.source: Although standard criteria would have classified all as playing an active role in stopping, 43% of cells with short-latency stop responses responded similarly or more strongly with sudden action initiation in switch-go trials.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the comparison of switch-stop and switch-go trials.

claims.claim: Stop and Switch cells did not overlap, categorically or anatomically, with the STN neurons most likely to be involved directly in the activation of antagonist muscles.
claims.source: These cells did not overlap, categorically or anatomically, with the STN neurons most likely to be involved directly in the activation of antagonist muscles, namely those responsive to proprioceptive stimulation and concentrated in the skeletomotor territory of the STN (Nambu et al., 2002; Parent and Hazrati, 1995; Baron et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This is a finding about the lack of overlap between cell types, with reference to previous literature on STN organization.

claims.claim: Schmidt et al. described a population of STN neurons in the rat that responded at short-latency to a Stop cue.
claims.source: Schmidt et al. (2013) described a population of STN neurons in the rat that responded at short-latency to a Stop cue.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of findings from a previous study.

claims.claim: In the Schmidt et al. study, STN neurons also responded at roughly equal latency and magnitude to the Go cue.
claims.source: Notably, unlike the present study, those neurons also responded at roughly equal latency and magnitude to the Go cue, which was presented on all trials (Mallet et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is a summary of findings from a previous study, contrasting with the present results.

claims.claim: Benis et al. described distinct sub-populations of STN neurons that responded selectively and at short latency to Stop and Go task signals in human subjects undergoing DBS surgery.
claims.source: In a recent study in human subjects undergoing DBS surgery for Parkinson's disease, Benis et al. (2016) described distinct sub-populations of STN neurons that responded selectively and at short latency to Stop and Go task signals, similar to our findings.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of findings from a previous study that are consistent with the present results.

claims.claim: Isoda and Hikosaka found a distinct sub-population of STN neurons that responded selectively and at short latency to an unexpected switch stimulus in macaques.
claims.source: Isoda and Hikosaka (2008) recorded from the macaque STN during a task that required animals to switch behaviors between familiar and unexpected oculomotor responses, somewhat similar to our switch-go type trials. Like us, they found a distinct sub-population of STN neurons that responded selectively and at short latency to the unexpected switch stimulus.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of findings from a previous study that are consistent with the present results.

claims.claim: No previous study dissociated STN activities related to reactive stopping, reactive switching and proactive (NoGo) response control.
claims.source: No previous study, however, dissociated STN activities related to reactive stopping, reactive switching and proactive (NoGo) response control, tested for potential overlap between stop-related activity and skeletomotor responsiveness, or addressed whether stop-related activity is concentrated in a sub-region of the STN.
claims.evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the present study compared to previous work.

claims.claim: Similar movement- and stop-related response patterns have been found in frontal eye cortex and superior colliculus of macaques performing an eye movement countermanding task.
claims.source: Finally, similar movement- and stop-related response patterns have been found in frontal eye cortex and superior colliculus of macaques performing an eye movement countermanding task (Schall and Godlove, 2012; Hanes et al., 1998; Paré and Hanes, 2003).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison to findings in other brain areas, supported by citations.

claims.claim: The STN includes an oculomotor territory.
claims.source: Although the STN includes an oculomotor territory (Matsumura et al., 1992), we found no evidence that the Stop-related activity identified here actually reflected movements of the eyes (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about STN organization supported by citation, followed by a negative finding from the present study.

claims.claim: Fully a quarter of STN neurons exhibited sustained activity preferentially after a NoGo cue.
claims.source: Fully a quarter of STN neurons exhibited sustained activity preferentially after a NoGo cue (Figure 8).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding about NoGo-related activity.

claims.claim: NoGo cells were not confined to a particular territory of the STN.
claims.source: These cells were not confined to a particular territory of the STN, a result that contrasted sharply with the anatomically-restricted location of stop cells.
claims.evidence: This is an anatomical finding contrasting NoGo cells with Stop cells.

claims.claim: The distribution of NoGo cells throughout the STN implies that many functional sub-circuits through the STN are activated during this behavior.
claims.source: The distribution of NoGo cells throughout the STN implies that many functional sub-circuits through the STN are activated during this behavior.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the anatomical distribution of NoGo cells.

claims.claim: Previous studies have implicated the striatum and the striato-pallidal-STN 'indirect' pathway in proactive control.
claims.source: Previous studies have implicated the striatum and the striato-pallidal-STN 'indirect' pathway in proactive control (Casey et al., 1997; Kelly et al., 2004; Smittenaar et al., 2013; Vink et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This is a summary of previous findings, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Proactive and reactive movement suppressions involve categorically different neural mechanisms.
claims.source: Although the present results do not address that possibility, they do argue that proactive and reactive movement suppressions involve categorically different neural mechanisms.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on the lack of overlap between Stop/Switch cells and NoGo cells.

claims.claim: The presence of NoGo activity in a single-unit had no predictive power over whether that unit also responded preferentially to switch-stop or switch-go signals.
claims.source: Not only were Stop and NoGo activities distributed differently within the STN, but the presence of NoGo activity in a single-unit had no predictive power over whether that unit also responded preferentially to switch-stop or switch-go signals (Figure 8E and Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is a finding about the independence of reactive and proactive cell types.

claims.claim: The STN receives topographically-organized glutamatergic inputs from most regions of the frontal cortex.
claims.source: The STN receives topographically-organized glutamatergic inputs from most regions of the frontal cortex (Nambu et al., 2002; Haynes and Haber, 2013; Monakow et al., 1978).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about STN connectivity supported by citations.

claims.claim: The inferior frontal cortex (IFC) has been linked closely to reactive stopping based on lesion and stimulation studies.
claims.source: Among these, the inferior frontal cortex (IFC; potential homologue in macaques: area 45) has been linked closely to reactive stopping based on lesion (Aron et al., 2003; Swick et al., 2008) and stimulation (Verbruggen et al., 2010; Wessel et al., 2013) studies.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of previous findings about IFC function, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Most prefrontal areas project to ventral and medial portions of the STN that encompass the regions where Stop and Switch cells were located.
claims.source: Although the specific topography of the IFC–to–STN projection has yet to be determined, tract-tracing studies indicate that most prefrontal areas [i.e., ventromedial, orbitofrontal, anterior cingulate and dorsal prefrontal cortices (Haynes and Haber, 2013)] project to ventral and medial portions of the STN that encompass the regions where Stop and Switch cells were located.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about STN connectivity based on previous tract-tracing studies, related to the present anatomical findings.

claims.claim: The ventromedial portion of STN receives strong GABAergic inputs from the rostral-medial external pallidum and ventral pallidum.
claims.source: This portion of the STN also receives strong GABAergic inputs from the rostral-medial external pallidum (part of the BG associative circuit) and ventral pallidum (of the BG limbic circuit) (Haynes and Haber, 2013; Shink et al., 1996; Karachi et al., 2005), and additional glutamatergic inputs from the parafascicular nucleus of the thalamus, also a limbic circuit-connected nucleus (Sadikot et al., 1992).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about STN connectivity supported by citations.

claims.claim: The ventromedial region of STN contained few cells with Movement-like activity.
claims.source: Consistent with its afferent connectivity, this ventromedial region contained few cells with Movement-like activity (Figure 4B), making it unlikely that Stop and Go processes are compared locally within the ventromedial STN.
claims.evidence: This is an anatomical finding with an interpretation about local processing.

claims.claim: A commonly accepted model states that the first efferent step from the STN is a highly divergent projection to the output nuclei of the BG.
claims.source: A commonly accepted model states that the first efferent step from the STN is a highly divergent projection to the output nuclei of the BG [i.e., internal pallidum (GPi) and SNr] (Aron, 2011; Aron and Poldrack, 2006; Schmidt et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is a description of a prevailing model, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Divergence in the STN-GPi/SNr pathway is said to be crucial for the broadcast of stop-related activity from the associative/limbic territory of the STN to GABAergic neurons in the skeletomotor and oculomotor territories of GPi and SNr.
claims.source: Divergence in this pathway is said to be crucial for the broadcast of stop-related activity from the associative/limbic territory of the STN to GABAergic neurons in the skeletomotor and oculomotor territories of GPi and SNr, respectively.
claims.evidence: This is a description of a theoretical mechanism in the prevailing model.

claims.claim: Limited evidence supports divergence in the STN-GPi/SNr pathway.
claims.source: Limited evidence supports divergence in the STN-GPi/SNr pathway, however (Hazrati and Parent, 1992), while multiple lines of evidence indicate instead that this axonal projection is highly specific and topographically organized (Shink et al., 1996; Smith et al., 1998; Kolomiets et al., 2001; Kelly and Strick, 2004; Miyachi et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is a critical evaluation of the prevailing model, supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claims.claim: Multiple lines of evidence indicate that the STN-GPi/SNr axonal projection is highly specific and topographically organized.
claims.source: Limited evidence supports divergence in the STN-GPi/SNr pathway, however (Hazrati and Parent, 1992), while multiple lines of evidence indicate instead that this axonal projection is highly specific and topographically organized (Shink et al., 1996; Smith et al., 1998; Kolomiets et al., 2001; Kelly and Strick, 2004; Miyachi et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about STN connectivity supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: Potential alternative pathways for STN stop signals include the direct STN projection to the tegmental pedunculopontine nucleus (PPN) and the disynaptic STN-GPi/SNr-PPN pathway.
claims.source: Potential alternative pathways include the direct STN projection to the tegmental pedunculopontine nucleus (PPN) (Shink et al., 1996; Hazrati and Parent, 1992; Parent and Smith, 1987; Nakano et al., 1990; Smith et al., 1990) as well as the disynaptic STN-GPi/SNr-PPN pathway.
claims.evidence: This is a proposal for alternative pathways, supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claims.claim: Selective activation of cholinergic neurons of the ventral PPN triggers a short-latency and wide-spread inhibition of motor output.
claims.source: It is interesting to note in this respect that selective activation of cholinergic neurons of the ventral PPN triggers a short-latency and wide-spread inhibition of motor output (Takakusaki et al., 1993; Takakusaki et al., 2016; Kohyama et al., 1998) in addition to a range of alerting and behavior-modulating functions (Mena-Segovia et al., 2004; Gut and Winn, 2016).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about PPN function supported by citations, relevant to the proposed alternative pathway.

claims.claim: It is quite likely that reactive stopping depends on a cascade of movement-suppressive processes and multiple brain pathways.
claims.source: And, as mentioned in the Introduction, it is quite likely that reactive stopping such as that studied here depends on a cascade of movement-suppressive processes and multiple brain pathways (Pouget et al., 2017; Schmidt and Berke, 2017).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the complexity of stopping mechanisms, supported by citations.

claims.claim: The STN influences motor control centers primarily via direct excitation of the GABAergic output neurons of the BG.
claims.source: Making sense of this type of activity is complicated by the widely-held view that the STN influences motor control centers primarily via direct excitation of the GABAergic output neurons of the BG (in GPi and SNr) (Nambu et al., 2002; Wichmann et al., 1994; Hamada and DeLong, 1992).
claims.evidence: This is a description of a prevailing view about STN function, supported by citations.

claims.claim: One recently-proposed solution is that another STN efferent pathway, which inhibits BG output neurons via a disynaptic pathway through the external pallidum (GPe), may dominate function of the circuit in certain behavioral contexts.
claims.source: One recently-proposed solution is that another STN efferent pathway, which inhibits BG output neurons via a disynaptic pathway through the external pallidum (GPe), may dominate function of the circuit in certain behavioral contexts (Jantz et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is a description of a recently proposed alternative model, supported by citation.

claims.claim: The present results concur in general terms with existing lines of evidence that implicate the ventromedial STN in various clinical disorders of inhibitory control.
claims.source: The present results concur in general terms with existing lines of evidence that implicate the ventromedial STN in various clinical disorders of inhibitory control.
claims.evidence: This is a statement connecting the present findings to clinical literature.

claims.claim: DBS in the ventral STN produces greater effects on inhibitory control behaviors than does stimulation in the dorsal STN.
claims.source: Case studies have shown that DBS in the ventral STN produces greater effects on inhibitory control behaviors than does stimulation in the dorsal STN (Greenhouse et al., 2013; Hershey et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is a summary of clinical findings, supported by citations.

claims.claim: The ventromedial STN is a current target for STN-DBS to treat severe obsessive compulsive disorder.
claims.source: In fact, this anatomic location is a current target for STN-DBS to treat severe obsessive compulsive disorder (Mallet et al., 2008), which is considered a disorder of inhibitory control.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about clinical practice, supported by citation.

claims.claim: Local micro-infusions of bicuculline (a GABA antagonist) only into the ventromedial part of the STN induced stereotypies and hyperactive behaviors.
claims.source: And local micro-infusions of bicuculline (a GABA antagonist) only into that part of the STN induced stereotypies and hyperactive behaviors (Karachi et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is a summary of a pharmacological study, supported by citation.

claims.claim: The present study is the first to show that single unit encoding of reactive stopping is restricted to the anterior ventromedial STN.
claims.source: The present study is the first to show that single unit encoding of reactive stopping also is restricted to the anterior ventromedial STN.
claims.evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the present findings.

claims.claim: Activity related to rapid response switching (Switch cells) was also confined to the same anatomic hotspot as Stop cells.
claims.source: It is interesting to note that activity related to rapid response switching (i.e., Switch cells) was also confined to the same anatomic hotspot (Figure 7C).

results.result: Monkeys performed a Go/NoGo-countermanding task with behavioral characteristics consistent with the race model of stop-signal tasks. Stop-failure trials had faster RTs than go trials, stop-failure probability increased with switch-signal delay, and the average SSRT was ~160 ms.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C24 describe the behavioral task and performance metrics. The data show expected patterns for stop-signal tasks (RT distributions, inhibition functions) with appropriate statistical support (Mann-Whitney U-tests, linear regressions). The SSRT estimates are slightly longer than previous studies but this is acknowledged and explained.

results.result: 38% of STN neurons (63/167) showed activity changes within the SSRT suitable for involvement in stopping. These included 78% Movement cells (49/63) with truncated movement-related activity and 22% Switch-stop cells (14/63) with phasic increases in firing. Neural cancellation times averaged −55 ms before SSRT.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C25-C29, C55 present the core neurophysiological findings with clear quantitative data and appropriate temporal criteria (neural cancellation within SSRT). The ROC analysis method is described and figures support the classification. Sample sizes are adequate for the reported proportions.

results.result: Switch-stop cells were anatomically segregated to the anterior ventromedial STN, a region known to receive inputs from associative/limbic cortical areas and implicated in impulse control disorders. This anatomical restriction was observed in both animals independently.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C30-C32, C94 describe the key anatomical finding shown in Figure 4B. The spatial segregation is clearly demonstrated, replicated across both subjects (C31), and connected to prior anatomical literature (C32). This represents a novel finding at the single-unit level (C94).

results.result: Of the 14 Switch-stop cells, 57% (8/14) were classified as Stop cells (selective for stopping), while 43% (6/14) were Switch cells (responding similarly to switch-go trials). Neural cancellation times did not differ between Stop and Switch cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C40, C61 describe further classification of Switch-stop cells based on comparison with switch-go trials. The proportions are clearly stated, the classification criteria are appropriate (comparing responses between conditions), and statistical tests support the lack of timing differences (p=0.66).

results.result: EMG recordings showed that arm movement inhibition involved rapid relaxation of agonists and brief activation of antagonists. STN neural cancellation times preceded most stop-related EMG changes (30-94 ms) except for the anterior deltoid (−10 ms, p>0.05).
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C37, C59 present EMG timing data relative to neural activity. While the muscle patterns are clearly shown (Figure 5A), the very short lead time for anterior deltoid (10 ms, non-significant) raises questions about whether STN activity could causally drive the earliest muscle changes. The authors acknowledge this timing constraint but the interpretation remains uncertain.

results.result: Switch-stop cell activity was not related to eye movements. Regression analyses found no Switch-stop cells (0/14) whose activity encoded eye position or saccade timing, despite the STN containing an oculomotor territory.
results.evaluation: Claims C41 and C69 address a potential confound. The regression analysis (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) appropriately tests for eye movement correlates using permutation tests (p>0.01). The negative finding is clearly stated and adequately controlled.

results.result: Torque-responsive neurons (25%, 42/167) were concentrated in dorsal posterolateral STN (skeletomotor territory). These showed minimal overlap with Switch-stop cells (only 1/42 was a Switch cell) and were anatomically distant from the ventromedial region containing Stop/Switch cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C46, C62 present proprioceptive control data. The spatial segregation between torque-responsive and Switch-stop cells (Figure 7C) is clear, the proportions are well-documented, and the minimal overlap (2%, 1/42) argues against Stop/Switch activity reflecting direct skeletomotor commands.

results.result: Proactive control was associated with distinct neuronal populations. Go cells (37%, 61/167) and NoGo cells (25%, 41/167) showed differential delay period activity but were distributed throughout STN without anatomical clustering, contrasting with the restricted localization of Stop cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C50, C70-C71 describe proactive control correlates. The behavioral evidence for proactive control is shown (C47, Figure 8—figure supplement 1), neuronal proportions are clearly stated, and the lack of anatomical clustering (Figure 8D) contrasts sharply with Stop cell localization, supporting distinct mechanisms.

results.result: Reactive and proactive control mechanisms are distinct in STN. No interaction was found between cell categories (χ²=1.75, p=0.42), Switch-stop cells were equally distributed between Go and NoGo categories, and NoGo activity had no predictive power for switch-signal responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C53, C74-C75 argue for independence of reactive and proactive mechanisms. The statistical test (χ² test) is appropriate, the proportions of Switch-stop cells in Go/NoGo categories are balanced (C52), and the lack of predictive relationship is demonstrated (Figure 8E, Figure 8—figure supplement 2).

results.result: Control analyses showed that reward- and error-related activities did not show similar anatomical localization to Stop cells, and baseline firing rates did not differ between cell types or animals.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C34 present negative control findings. The lack of anatomical clustering for reward/error signals (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) contrasts with Stop cell localization, and the ANOVA (F<2.13, p>0.15) appropriately tests for baseline differences. These controls strengthen the main findings.

results.result: The study provides the first evidence for selective encoding of reactive stopping at the cellular level in healthy primate STN, restricted to the ventromedial portion. This finding is consistent with clinical evidence implicating this region in impulse control disorders and DBS effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C54, C67, C90-C93 present the main conclusions and clinical relevance. The novelty claims (C54, C67) are justified by the comprehensive dissociation of stopping, switching, and proactive control. The connection to clinical literature (C90-C93) is well-supported by citations and aligns with the anatomical findings.

results.result: Two distinct response patterns were observed among STN neurons meeting temporal criteria: Movement cells with truncated movement-related activity (most common) and cells with phasic increases to stop signals. Movement cell cancellation times were slightly earlier than Stop cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C58 describe the two main response patterns. The patterns are clearly illustrated (Figures 3-4), the relative timing is quantified (C58), and the interpretation that Movement cells show earlier cancellation is data-driven, though it challenges simple race model predictions.

results.result: The ventromedial STN region containing Stop/Switch cells receives topographically organized inputs from prefrontal cortex (including IFC linked to stopping), GABAergic inputs from associative/limbic pallidum, and contained few Movement cells, making local comparison of Stop and Go processes unlikely.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C80 integrate the present anatomical findings with prior connectivity literature. The citations to tract-tracing studies are appropriate (C76-C79), and the observation that this region contains few Movement cells (C80, Figure 4B) is data-driven and leads to a reasonable inference about local processing.

results.result: The commonly accepted model of divergent STN projections to GPi/SNr has limited anatomical support. Alternative pathways including direct and indirect STN-PPN projections may mediate stop signals, and reactive stopping likely depends on multiple pathways and cascaded processes.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C87 critically evaluate prevailing models and propose alternatives. The critique of the divergence model is well-supported by anatomical citations (C83-C84), the PPN pathway proposal is grounded in anatomy and physiology (C85-C86), and the acknowledgment of multiple pathways (C87) is appropriately cautious.

results.result: Comparison with prior studies shows both similarities and differences. Unlike rat STN recordings where neurons responded equally to Stop and Go cues, the present study found selective responses. Human DBS studies and macaque oculomotor studies found similar selective populations.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C66, C68 appropriately contextualize findings within prior literature. The contrasts with rat studies (C63-C64) and similarities with human/primate studies (C65-C66, C68) are accurately represented based on the citations. This demonstrates both novelty and consistency with relevant prior work.

results.result: Background claims establish that STN is hypothesized to play a central role in stopping based on neuroimaging, lesion, and DBS studies, though prior single-unit evidence was limited and potentially confounded. STN has distinct anatomical subdivisions with the ventromedial region receiving prefrontal inputs.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C6-C18 provide background context supported by appropriate citations. These establish the motivation for the study, summarize prior evidence for STN involvement in stopping, and describe relevant anatomical organization. The citations appear accurate and comprehensive.

results.result: Interpretive claims about STN function: STN is part of attention/salience networks, NoGo cell distribution implies multiple functional sub-circuits, prior studies implicated indirect pathway in proactive control, and STN influences motor centers primarily via GPi/SNr excitation though GPe-mediated inhibition may dominate in some contexts.
results.evaluation: Claims C60, C72-C73, C88-C89 present interpretations and connections to broader literature. These are appropriately supported by citations and represent reasonable inferences from the data (e.g., C72 about NoGo cell distribution). The acknowledgment of alternative models (C89) shows appropriate scientific caution.

results.result: Ethical approval was obtained from the University of Pittsburgh IACUC (protocol 12111162) and procedures complied with Public Health Service policies.
results.evaluation: Claim C96 documents ethical approval. This is a straightforward statement of regulatory compliance that is standard for animal research and does not require further evaluation.
